clue.text: Crashed motor? Argument in the near future

indicators.note: a crashed motor is a wrecked one, so its letters are knocked out of order

explanation.surface: Someone's car has been written off and a quarrel is looming.
explanation.walkthrough: The question mark splits the clue: the crash and the row look like one story, but they are two separate pieces laid end to end.
explanation.definitionFit: TOMORROW, used loosely as an adverb, means soon or in the near future.

clue.text: Objection raised over a brass instrument

indicators.note: in a down entry, raising a word turns it upside down, reading it bottom to top
in a down entry, one part sits over (above) the next

parts.note: a but = an objection, as in 'no buts'

explanation.surface: Someone is complaining about a loud brass instrument, perhaps a neighbour's practice.
explanation.walkthrough: 'But' as a noun is an objection, as in 'no ifs or buts'.
explanation.definitionFit: A definition by example: the tuba is one member of the brass family, its lowest voice.

clue.text: Timid? Startled cry after first sign of mouse

indicators.note: the first sign of a word is its opening letter

parts.note: eek! is the stock startled cry

explanation.surface: A timid person shrieks at the sight of a mouse.
explanation.walkthrough: The clue writes the cartoon scene of someone screaming at a mouse; the cry itself is the letters.
explanation.definitionFit: Meek means quiet, gentle and easily cowed, i.e. timid.

clue.text: No German will get upset about one area

indicators.note: in a down entry, upsetting a word tips it over so it reads bottom to top
the reversed letters go around the next piece

parts.note: GER is the standard abbreviation for German

explanation.surface: A German's refusal leaves someone annoyed about a region.
explanation.walkthrough: The German's 'no' looks like it should be NEIN; here the two words are taken separately, and the pair is flipped before the one goes in.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: both words name a stretch of land or part of the world.

clue.text: Someone caring for nippers relishing a toy, possibly

indicators.note: the letters could possibly be arranged as something else

explanation.surface: A childminder is looking after small children who love playing with a toy.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Nippers' reads as young children, the childminder's charges; here it means teeth, which nip.
explanation.definitionFit: An oral hygienist cleans and cares for teeth, playfully called nippers.

clue.text: Nurse, perhaps, needing extra energy in vocation

indicators.note: the carer needs something added to make the answer

parts.note: a nurse is one kind of carer

explanation.surface: Nursing is described as a calling that demands extra energy.
explanation.walkthrough: CARER takes E into its middle: CAR(E)ER. The surface pairs nursing and vocation so the definition feels like part of the story.
explanation.definitionFit: A career is one's chosen vocation or profession.

clue.text: New party invested in a transport system without purpose

indicators.note: money invested in something is put into it

explanation.surface: A new political party puts money into a tram network with no clear aim.
explanation.walkthrough: N and DO go into A TRAM: A TRA(NDO)M. 'Party' looks political, but it is a social do.
explanation.definitionFit: Doing something at random means doing it with no plan or aim, so a plain synonym for purposeless.

clue.text: Oddly view six clues, cryptic — you won't find them in other papers!

definitions.text: you won't find them in other papers!

indicators.note: cryptic means puzzling, so the letters are jumbled
take the odd-numbered letters

explanation.surface: The setter boasts of six puzzle clues that no rival paper prints.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Six' is not VI here; all three of its letters join the fodder.
explanation.definitionFit: Exclusives are stories one paper has that no other paper carries.

clue.text: Store? Ropy store I rebuilt

indicators.note: rebuilding puts the letters together a new way

explanation.surface: A shopkeeper says they rebuilt a shabby shop.
explanation.walkthrough: The setter deliberately reuses 'store': once as the definition, again inside the fodder. 'Ropy' is British for poor quality.
explanation.definitionFit: A repository is a place where things are stored.

clue.text: Elizabeth will swallow variety of lager in this!

definitions.text: Elizabeth will swallow variety of lager in this!

indicators.note: the outer name takes the other letters inside it
a variety is a different form, so the letters are rearranged

explanation.surface: Elizabeth is about to down some kind of lager from her glass.
explanation.walkthrough: The exclamation mark flags that the whole clue does double duty: read plainly, it describes the vessel Elizabeth drinks her lager from.
explanation.definitionFit: Read straight, the whole clue describes the vessel: lager goes into it before being swallowed.

clue.text: A lot of fish without any variety — many a kid will get stuck into that

definitions.text: many a kid will get stuck into that

parts.note: a school is a large group of fish

explanation.surface: A shoal of identical fish, which children love poking at.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Stuck into' reads as eager tucking in; here it means getting dressed in the clothes.
explanation.definitionFit: Many children put on a school uniform every morning.

clue.text: Summary regarding EU farming policy

explanation.surface: A briefing summarises European agricultural policy.
explanation.walkthrough: CAP is the EU's Common Agricultural Policy, which funds farmers.
explanation.definitionFit: A recap is a brief summary of what went before.

clue.text: Host party before twice-yearly awards?

indicators.note: one part comes before the next

parts.note: the British honours lists come out twice a year

explanation.surface: Someone throws a party ahead of an awards ceremony.
explanation.walkthrough: The British Honours list (knighthoods, OBEs and the like) is published twice a year, at New Year and on the monarch's birthday.
explanation.definitionFit: To do the honours is to act as host, serving drinks or food to guests.

clue.text: No French song about US city will be carefree

indicators.note: the song goes around the city

explanation.surface: A French song about an American city has a relaxed air.
explanation.walkthrough: NON + CHA(LA)NT, with LA tucked into CHANT.
explanation.definitionFit: Nonchalant means calm and unconcerned, i.e. carefree.

clue.text: British farm left in trouble, ultimately — no major transport access

indicators.note: 'ultimately' means in the end, so only the end letter of the word is used

explanation.surface: A British farm is left in difficulty because it has no main road.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface reads as one farm's hard luck; each word is a separate letter or chunk.
explanation.definitionFit: A branch line is a minor railway line off the main line.

clue.text: Monster, cornered by another goblin, retreating

indicators.note: trapped inside the words that follow
going backwards, so read right to left

explanation.surface: A monster is trapped in a corner by a goblin and backs away.
explanation.walkthrough: ERGO sits across the two words, and read backwards it spells the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: An ogre is a man-eating monster of folklore.

clue.text: Land manager redistributed most grain, keeping nothing in stock

indicators.note: the letters are shared out again in a new order

parts.note: nothing = O, the stock of letters keeps it

explanation.surface: A farm manager redistributed most of the grain and kept nothing in reserve.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Most' is not a truncation signal here; its letters are part of the fodder.
explanation.definitionFit: An agronomist is an expert in soil and crop management.

clue.text: Support for text showing American car and its maximum capacity?

parts.note: a fill is the full amount something holds

explanation.surface: A text document described with an American car and its top capacity.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Text' suggests printed words; the definition is the software feature that completes typing for you.
explanation.definitionFit: Autofill supports typing text by filling in the rest of a word or form.

clue.text: Evoked criminal before jury, not half awful prude

indicators.note: before places the criminal ahead of the rest

parts.note: a con is a convict, a criminal

indicators.note: not half means only half the word survives, so jury loses its second half

parts.note: taken as written before it is halved

indicators.note: awful means dreadful or messed up, so the letters of prude are rearranged

parts.note: taken as written before it is rearranged

explanation.surface: A courtroom scene: a crook in the dock, with a strait-laced juror looking on aghast.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface pairs 'criminal' with 'jury' as a trial, but each is a separate piece: 'not half' keeps only the first two letters of jury, and 'awful' is the signal to rearrange prude.
explanation.definitionFit: To conjure up is to call to mind or summon an image or memory, which is what evoking means.

clue.text: Fruit-tree, source of plums, getting attention

indicators.note: the source of a word is its first letter

parts.note: to have someone's ear is to have their attention

explanation.surface: An orchard tree is noticed for its plums.
explanation.walkthrough: The plums seem to belong to the tree; only their first letter is used.
explanation.definitionFit: The fruit's name doubles as the tree's name, as with apple or plum.

clue.text: Sarcastic US spies turned up, apprehending detectives

indicators.note: in a down entry, turning up reverses the letters to read bottom to top
catching, so holding the next piece inside

parts.note: the Criminal Investigation Department of British police

explanation.surface: Scornful American agents show up and arrest some detectives.
explanation.walkthrough: CIA turned up gives AIC, which holds CID: A(CID)IC.
explanation.definitionFit: Acidic remarks are sharp and biting, i.e. sarcastic.

clue.text: Disco pariahs, dancing to create ways of increasing desire

indicators.note: dancing letters move about into a new order

explanation.surface: Social outcasts dance at a disco in an effort to become more attractive.
explanation.walkthrough: The disco setting makes the answer feel at home.
explanation.definitionFit: Aphrodisiacs are things that increase sexual desire.

clue.text: Perhaps Basil and Sybil's central feature?

definitions.meaning: first meaning: basil is one example of a culinary plant of this kind
second meaning, read playfully as the answer: the B is the letter at the centre of Sybil's name

explanation.surface: A nod to Fawlty Towers, whose hotelier Basil is married to Sybil.
explanation.walkthrough: Basil and Sybil Fawlty run the hotel in the British sitcom Fawlty Towers. The second sense splits the answer as HER B, the B at the centre of Sybil's name.
explanation.definitionFit: Basil is a leafy plant used for flavouring, so an instance of the answer, flagged by 'Perhaps'.

clue.text: US prize? Judge resigning from prize in US

indicators.note: a judge resigning from the word leaves it, so its letter is taken out

parts.note: prize is the American spelling of prise, to lever open, which is what you do with a jemmy

explanation.surface: A quiz question about an American award and a judge stepping down from its panel.
explanation.walkthrough: A jemmy is the British name for a burglar's short crowbar, and to jemmy is to force open, spelt prize in the US and prise in Britain. Remove J for judge.
explanation.definitionFit: The Emmy is the annual American award for excellence in television.

clue.text: Liberal put in excellent explanation for absence

indicators.note: one piece is put inside the other

explanation.surface: A Liberal politician is given a fine excuse for not showing up.
explanation.walkthrough: A1 is written with the 1 as the letter I, giving A(LIB)I.
explanation.definitionFit: An alibi is proof that one was somewhere else at the time.

clue.text: Norwegian city starts to tempt reclusive US composer? Not at first

indicators.note: the starts of the two words are their first letters

parts.note: these two words supply their first letters

indicators.note: the composer is not there at first, so his name loses its opening letter

parts.note: Stephen Sondheim was the American composer of Sweeney Todd and Into the Woods

explanation.surface: Someone hoping to lure a shy American songwriter to Norway.
explanation.walkthrough: 'starts to' gives T and R; Stephen Sondheim, minus his first letter by 'Not at first', gives ONDHEIM.
explanation.definitionFit: Trondheim is a historic port in central Norway, once the country's capital.

clue.text: Boy soprano's a good bet?

definitions.meaning: the highest voice in a church choir, sung by boys
a betting term: one wager on three selections at once

explanation.surface: Someone suggests backing a young choirboy to succeed.
explanation.walkthrough: A treble in betting is a single bet on three selections, all of which must win.
explanation.definitionFit: A treble is a boy with a soprano voice, and also a three-part bet.

clue.text: Taxi in Peruvian city backed up to yard in a friendly way

indicators.note: the taxi goes inside the city
backed up means reversed, so the city reads right to left

explanation.surface: A taxi in Lima reverses up to a yard in a courteous manner.
explanation.walkthrough: AMIL holds CAB, then Y is added: AMI(CAB)L + Y.
explanation.definitionFit: Amicably means in a friendly, goodwill manner.
